name: Charminar
historicalSignificance: Constructed as one of the earliest edifices in the newly founded city of Hyderabad on 1 Muharram 1000 AH (1591–92 CE) by Sultan Mohammad Quli Qutub Shah, fifth ruler of the Qutub Shahi dynasty.
architecturalStyle: Qutub Shahi stone and lime-mortar square monument (31.95 m) with four 56 m minarets, cardinal arches, arcaded gallery, second-floor mosque, and stucco ornamentation

preservationInformation.custodian: Archaeological Survey of India (Hyderabad Circle)
preservationInformation.statusSummary: Managed as a principal protected monument (Monument Code 5.5.2) under the Archaeological Survey of India’s Hyderabad Circle; recorded restoration works include rebuilding the south-western minaret after lightning damage, complete lime re-plastering in 1824 CE under Asaf Jah III, and mechanical maintenance of the 1889 facade clocks (repaired in 1962).

description: Iconic 1591–92 CE Qutub Shahi civic edifice and mosque in Hyderabad built of stone and lime mortar on a 31.95 m square plan with four cardinal arches, a second-floor mosque containing 45 prayer spaces, delicate stucco decoration, and four corner minarets rising 56 m from ground level.

name: Rani Ki Vav
alternativeNames: Rani-ki-Vav (the Queen’s Stepwell) at Patan, Gujarat
historicalSignificance: Built on the banks of the Saraswati River as a memorial to a king, representing the height of stepwell construction and Maru-Gurjara architectural craftsmanship.
architecturalStyle: Maru-Gurjara architectural style subterranean stepwell designed as an inverted temple with seven levels of stairs

preservationInformation.custodian: Archaeological Survey of India
preservationInformation.statusSummary: Formally designated an Ancient Monument of National Importance under the AMASR Act (1958, 2010 Amendment) and administered solely by the Archaeological Survey of India under a Superintending Archaeologist and on-site team with a 100 m non-development zone and active ASI management plan (commenced 2013), with UNESCO advising enhanced seismic risk preparedness.

description: An 11th-century subterranean stepwell in Patan, Gujarat built in the Maru-Gurjara architectural style and designed as an inverted temple with seven levels of stairs, over 500 principal sculptures, and a 30-m deep well shaft.
